Dear Secretary Reese:   
Pursuant to section 205 of the Federal Power Act (“FPA”), Pacific Gas and Electric 
Company (“PG&E”) submits amendments to its Transmission Owners Tariff, FERC Electric 
Tariff Volume No. 5 (“TO Tariff”), to address the issues identified by the Federal Energy 
Regulatory Commission (“Commission” or “FERC”) as potentially unjust and unreasonable in 
its Order to Show Cause (“OSC”) issued in Docket No. EL26-71-000.1  Specifically, PG&E 
proposes changes to its TO Tariff to implement a process that will enable Transmission 
Customers for Large Load (“TCLLs”) to interconnect “Large Load End Users” to the PG&E 
transmission system.  The process will ensure that the necessary transmission facilities are in 
place to provide the interconnection and transmission service required for the TCLLs to serve 
those customers.2  PG&E’s proposed TO Tariff amendments and this filing are submitted in 
response to and answer the OSC pursuant to section 206 of the FPA, 16 U.S.C. § 824e, Rule 213 
of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure, and Ordering Paragraph B of the OSC.   
PG&E requests that the Commission find the proposed changes to the TO Tariff just and 
reasonable and that the changes address the issues raised in the OSC.  PG&E notes that the 
CAISO is proposing amendments to the CAISO Open Access Transmission Tariff (“CAISO 
Tariff”) to address the issues raised in the OSC regarding the CAISO Tariff.  PG&E requests that 
the Commission accept the proposed changes effective February 16, 2027, the same day that the

I. 
INTRODUCTION 
The California Energy Commission (“CEC”) forecasts that data center load in the CAISO 
BAA will increase by 1.8 gigawatts (“GW”) by 2030 and 4.9 GW by 2040.3  In recent years, 
PG&E has received substantially more applications from large load customers seeking 
transmission-level interconnections.4  The OSC arises from this increase in large load.   
On June 18, 2026, the Commission issued the OSC in Docket No. EL26-71 as one of six-
region specific orders to show cause addressing the unprecedented growth of large loads.5  The 
Commission instituted this proceeding to address the “urgent challenges associated with 
providing the transmission service needed to serve the ongoing influx of large loads while 
maintaining reliability and affordability,” including concerns that large loads are not efficiently 
integrated onto the transmission system, that they pose unique reliability challenges, and that the 
rates, terms, and conditions of transmission service may not remain just and reasonable as large 
loads are added.6  The OSC preliminarily finds that the CAISO Tariff and the TO Tariffs may 
lack the provisions needed to provide transmission service to TCLLs reliably, affordably, and 
without shifting costs to other transmission customers.7  The OSC’s preliminary findings reflect 
four related policy objectives.   
The first is reliability.  The OSC finds that large loads can be more energy-intensive and 
geographically concentrated than other load growth and can affect the transmission system in

operational requirements tailored to their characteristics.8  The second is timely and efficient 
integration.  The OSC seeks application study processes with defined timelines and readiness 
requirements that deter speculative or duplicative requests, which can delay studies, distort load 
forecasts, and lead to unnecessary network upgrades, and it directs the evaluation of alternative 
transmission technologies that can add capacity more quickly and at lower cost.9  The third is 
protection of transmission customers.  The Commission seeks transparency regarding the 
network upgrades and costs needed to serve large loads, and a cost recovery agreement to ensure 
that transmission customers serving large loads bear their fair share of the costs to provide 
transmission service to those loads.10  The fourth is flexibility.  The OSC notes that “load 
flexibility can avoid inefficient and costly transmission system build-out.”11 Accordingly, the 
Commission seeks tariff provisions that offer transmission services, with regional variation as 
appropriate, that reflect “the use of the transmission system by Eligible Customers on behalf of 
flexible large load, on both an interim and permanent basis.”12 In ordering these directives to be 
met, however, the OSC acknowledges that the CAISO framework “is unique among the 
RTOs/ISOs” and that certain responsibilities fall to the Participating Transmission Owners 
(“PTOs” or “Participating TOs”), and the Commission does not seek to alter the allocation of 
responsibilities between the CAISO and the PTOs.13 
PG&E’s proposal responds to each of these concerns within the CAISO’s existing 
structure and provides a clear, standardized framework that the growth of large loads in PG&E’s 
service territory and the CAISO more broadly requires.  Because the CAISO does not offer 
traditional stand-alone transmission service, PG&E proposes to implement the OSC’s directives 
primarily through a new Section 10A of its TO Tariff that governs the interconnection of TCLLs 
to the transmission system on behalf of their Large Load End Users.  PG&E also proposes to 
implement four new pro forma agreements, which can be found in Appendix XI of PG&E’s TO 
Tariff.14  Specifically, PG&E proposes:  (1) an application process with readiness requirements, 
and separate Serial and Cluster Study processes for Electrically Independent and Electrically 
Dependent Large Loads; (2) an Agreement to Interconnect Transmission Customer for Large 
Load (“TCLL Agreement”) memorializing the TCLL Interconnection; (3) a Facilities Agreement 
governing construction and the cost responsibility framework for Direct Assignment and TCLL 
Interconnection Network Upgrades and expansions; (4) a Cost Assurance Agreement that 
protects other transmission customers from cost shifting associated with TCLL Reliability 
Network Upgrades; and (5) a voluntary Interim Service Agreement that allows a TCLL to permit 
Large Load End Users to begin taking Flexible Interim Large Load Interconnection Service

In developing these proposals, PG&E coordinated with the other Participating TOs in the 
CAISO footprint.  PG&E and Southern California Edison Company (“SCE”) reached broad 
consensus on the cost responsibility and flexible service frameworks adopted in their respective 
proposals.  PG&E is also aligned with San Diego Gas & Electric Company (“SDG&E”) and LS 
Power Grid California, LLC (“LS Power”) on requiring a financial mechanism to protect against 
the risk of cost shifting due to speculative or departing loads.  PG&E’s proposed changes provide 
the clarity, consistency, and protection the OSC seeks.  They also preserve the CAISO’s 
Transmission Planning Process (“TPP”) as the primary means by which the CAISO plans the 
system to serve aggregate Load growth, including Large Loads, and preserve the coordinated 
roles of the CAISO and the Participating TOs.   
For these reasons and the reasons set forth below, PG&E requests that the Commission 
find the proposed changes to the TO Tariff just and reasonable and that the changes address the 
issues raised in the OSC. 
II. 
BACKGROUND 
A. 
CAISO Is a Unique Transmission Market That Does Not Operate in 
the Same Manner as Other RTOs.  
The OSC recognizes that “the framework under which CAISO provides transmission 
service is unique among the RTOs/ISOs and that certain responsibilities fall to the Participating 
Transmission Owners.”15  Most other regions operate under the traditional framework 
established in Order No. 888.  There, the Commission required all public utilities that own, 
operate, or control interstate transmission facilities to offer network and point-to-point 
transmission services to all Eligible Customers under a pro forma open access transmission 
tariff, and established “rules for discounting practices, provisions governing priority of service 
and curtailment, and a right of first refusal for all firm transmission customers.”16  That 
framework is based on advance reservations of transmission capacity by transmission customers.  
A transmission customer, including the transmission provider, may reserve existing capacity for 
native and network load growth, and the customer may secure firm transmission service ahead of

As the OSC recognizes, the CAISO’s framework differs from this traditional framework 
in several key ways.  The CAISO’s transmission service model has no formal application process 
for transmission service, and wholesale transmission customers do not reserve transmission 
capacity in advance.19  Instead, Scheduling Coordinators—entities certified by the CAISO to 
submit balanced schedules on behalf of customers20—submit bids or self-schedules for supply 
and demand into the CAISO day-ahead and real-time markets, with equal access to all available 
transmission capacity each day.   If available transmission capacity is insufficient, losing bidders 
cannot schedule service.  If in real-time all accepted schedules cannot be met, due to unexpected 
or unplanned events, the CAISO curtails schedules based on tariff-defined scheduling 
priorities.21   
Unlike a traditional network customer, the Scheduling Coordinator does not reserve, or 
pay for, transmission service on behalf of a specific Load.  Nor does the Scheduling Coordinator 
pay an access charge for scheduling and settling Load on behalf of Eligible Customers.  Rather, 
the CAISO Tariff assesses Regional and Local Access Charges on each UDC or MSS, as 
Eligible Customers, represented by a Scheduling Coordinator to serve Load.  As a result, the 
functions of a single network customer requesting service in other RTOs are divided among, and 
coordinated between, the PTOs, Scheduling Coordinators, and UDCs and MSSs.   
Under this unique framework, the CAISO does not refer to wholesale transmission 
customers as “Eligible Customers” in the same way as the OSC.22  Rather, in the CAISO, an 
“Eligible Customer” is the UDC or MSS that procures transmission service and provides service 
to Large Load End Users.23  PG&E is therefore proposing terminology tailored to how 
transmission service is provided to the same wholesale transmission customers referenced in the

B. 
CAISO and the PTOs Each Perform Unique and Coordinated 
Functions with Respect to Requests to Interconnect to the 
Transmission System  
Participating TOs are responsible for studying requests from customers with Wholesale 
Load to interconnect to the CAISO-controlled transmission system (“CAISO Controlled Grid”) 
or increase or modify the nature or number of delivery points to serve such Load as it grows 
under the TO Tariff.26  PG&E’s Wholesale Load Interconnection service is coordinated with the 
CAISO, which provides Market Access and Generation (i.e., resource) interconnection service to 
such Wholesale Load.27  This coordinated framework supports the respective tariff 
responsibilities of the Participating TOs and the CAISO under the Transmission Control 
Agreement and ensures that Wholesale Load Interconnections are studied, planned, and 
implemented consistent with transmission reliability requirements and long-term transmission 
plans.28  Applicants seeking wholesale generation interconnection to the CAISO Controlled Grid 
submit their requests to the CAISO, while applicants seeking Wholesale Load Interconnection 
submit their requests to the relevant Participating TO.29   
The CAISO reviews the impacts of all new Load interconnections and increases in Load 
growth using two related processes.  The first is the annual TPP conducted under Section 24 of 
the CAISO Tariff.  The TPP is the process the CAISO uses to plan the transmission system and 
approve transmission solutions, including constructing new transmission facilities and network 
upgrades, to serve load growth within the CAISO footprint.30  The TPP integrates the CEC 
statewide long-term energy demand forecast and the CPUC’s integrated resource planning 
information, both of which consider and account for large loads.31  The second is the CAISO’s 
“concurrence” process, which allows the Participating TOs to propose transmission solutions and

C. 
PG&E and the Other Founding Transmission Owning Members of 
CAISO Have Unique and Specific Roles. 
PG&E is one of the three Original Participating Transmission Owners (“Original 
Participating TOs”) that transferred Operational Control of their transmission facilities to the 
CAISO while retaining ownership, physical operation, and maintenance responsibilities of those 
facilities.  The Original Participating TOs have a distinct position within the CAISO market 
structure.   
Like the other Original Participating TOs, PG&E must purchase transmission service for 
all retail customers within its service territory.  Most retail customers located in the CAISO BAA 
interconnect to distribution facilities owned by a UDC or MSS under retail tariffs approved by 
the Local Regulatory Authority, or the California Public Utilities Commission (“CPUC”), if the 
utility is investor-owned.  These retail tariffs govern the study costs, retail rates, and potential 
cost recovery for retail Load interconnections.37  However, when the MSS or UDC is not a PTO, 
the MSS or UDC must seek Wholesale Load Interconnection service through the Participating 
TO Tariff to provide transmission service to those retail customers.  As an Original Participating 
TO, PG&E is not a wholesale transmission customer on its transmission system and is not

D. 
The OSC Preliminarily Found the CAISO and TO Tariffs to Be Unjust 
and Unreasonable as They Pertain to Eligible Customers Serving 
Large Loads.

as appropriate, to develop responses to this order.”42  Consistent with that direction, the CAISO

III. 
PG&E SUPPORTS THE CAISO’S PROPOSED DEFINITION OF LARGE LOAD 
AS BEING JUST AND REASONABLE. 
A. 
The OSC Requires a Definition of Large Load Sufficient to Capture 
the Loads That Present the Unique Challenges to the Transmission 
System Identified in the OSC. 
The OSC preliminarily found that the CAISO Tariff and/or the TO Tariffs appear to be 
unjust and unreasonable because they lack “a definition of large load, as a new category of 
load.”45  As the Commission explained, integrating large loads poses specific challenges 
because, although large loads are retail customers, they can impact reliability on the transmission 
system in ways comparable to large wholesale generators.46  The OSC therefore directs that an 
appropriate definition, including load size, be adopted.  The OSC also notes that the definition 
should be based on the characteristics of CAISO’s transmission system.47 
Importantly, the OSC did not mandate a particular definition.  Rather, the Commission 
identified, based on the record in the Large Load Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking 
proceeding, a definition that it preliminarily found would be reasonable:  
a new commercial or industrial customer, located at a single site 
behind one or more points of interconnection, that has a peak load

B. 
PG&E Supports and Adopts CAISO’s Proposed Definition of Large 
Load Because it Meets the Requirements of the OSC While 
Maintaining the Unique Aspects of the CAISO Transmission System.  
In response to the OSC, PG&E proposes to amend its TO Tariff to adopt the CAISO’s 
proposed definition of Large Load.  CAISO proposes to define Large Load as “an End User 
located at a single site or behind one or more point(s) of interconnection to the CAISO 
Controlled Grid, and that has a peak load of 50 MW or greater.”50  This definition satisfies the 
OSC’s requirements.  It adopts the 50 MW peak-load threshold and includes Large Loads that 
are interconnecting behind the CAISO Controlled Grid and that have a Point of Withdrawal on 
the CAISO Controlled Grid for taking transmission service.51  
The CAISO’s proposed definition appropriately captures the transmission-service 
relationship at issue in the OSC, while avoiding an artificial requirement that the end user 
connect directly to the grid.52  The vast majority of Large Loads in the CAISO do not connect 
directly to the CAISO-Controlled Grid.  Rather, Large Loads typically connect to the 
Distribution Systems of their TCLL.  However, those Large Loads have an impact on the 
transmission system when the TCLL seeks interconnection and transmission service to serve the 
Large Load End User.  The proposed definition encompasses the Large Load that the OSC 
intended to reach and therefore appropriately addresses the Commission’s concerns.  The

IV. 
PG&E PROPOSES JUST AND REASONABLE CHANGES TO ITS TARIFF TO 
IMPLEMENT A NEW APPLICATION AND STUDY PROCESS FOR TCLLS 
INTERCONNECTING LARGE LOAD END USERS TO THE PG&E 
TRANSMISSION SYSTEM. 
As discussed in Section II, the CAISO does not offer Order No. 888 network or point-to-
point transmission service, does not accept advance reservations of transmission capacity, and 
has no formal application process for transmission service.55 Identifying the necessary 
transmission facilities needed to accommodate new Loads interconnecting to the transmission 
system through UDCs and MSSs is conducted through either the TO Tariff or the CAISO TPP 
Process.  The CAISO conducts the TPP pursuant to Section 24 of the CAISO Tariff to identify 
transmission solutions needed for the CAISO system, including maintaining system reliability 
and reducing congestion.56  Participating TOs study interconnection requests under the TO Tariff 
and, where reliability network upgrades and network upgrades are implicated, either seek the 
CAISO’s concurrence that the project is a transmission facility that should be included in the

execute a CAISO pro forma Participating Generator Agreement for the generating facility, but

and other public power service area rights.  Indeed, co-location itself may be rare in the CAISO, 
given state laws on when a retail seller is deemed to be a CPUC-jurisdictional electrical 
corporation, subject to CPUC rate regulation and myriad other California laws and CPUC 
regulation.172  In CPUC-regulated utility service areas, renewable and cogeneration generators 
are permitted in limited circumstances to serve up to two retail loads without being regulated by

that required PG&E to add new processes for Large Load also evidenced the fact certain portions 
of the TO Tariff had not always been revised through the past nearly three decades in a manner 
that kept it congruent with the CAISO Tariff.  Thus, PG&E has revised the body of its TO Tariff 
in a variety of ways.175   
First, PG&E observed that Section 1 no longer reflected Appendix F of the CAISO Tariff 
regarding how in-BAA transmission service was paid for.  Section 1 also was the first section 
that indicated that PG&E had not adopted the CAISO’s “Regional” and “Local” vernacular 
rather than “High Voltage” and “Low Voltage.”  The sets of terms are identical, and the

submitted a completed application for retail service before the original effective date of Section

for Wholesale Load Interconnection Applications.  In addition, PG&E requests an effective date 
of February 16, 2027, which, together with the annual Cluster Study timing in Section 10A.5.1,
